page: Amazon Web Services x1e.4xlarge is a memory-optimized instance built on the Xen hypervisor and x86_64 architecture. It provides 16 dedicated vCPUs across 8 physical cores running on an Intel Xeon E7-8880 v3 processor clocked at 2.3 GHz. The instance includes 32 KB L1d cache, 0.25 MB L2 cache, and 45 MB L3 cache per socket structure. It features an exceptionally large memory allocation of 488.0 GB, yielding 30.5 GB of RAM per vCPU. Storage is addressed via an included 480 GB local SSD, while baseline network throughput is rated at 2 Gbps without dedicated GPU hardware.

Benchmark results highlight an architecture oriented toward memory capacity rather than raw compute speed. Single-core performance falls in lower percentiles, demonstrated by a stress-ng single-core score of 739.29 and a Geekbench single-core score of 797.0. Multi-core performance reaches middle percentiles, recording 8296.17 on stress-ng, 4537.0 on Geekbench multi-core, and 11161.62 on PassMark CPU. While cached small-block memory reads achieve 624.32 GB/sec, large-block uncached read and write bandwidths measure 14.66 GB/sec and 11.2 GB/sec respectively. Synthetic database operations show steady mid-tier execution, including 9.47 million Redis SET operations per second and a PassMark database score of 3868.29.

Given its massive memory footprint paired with moderate compute throughput, the x1e.4xlarge represents a specialized cost-efficiency model where hardware expenses are concentrated almost entirely in memory capacity. It is suboptimal for compute-intensive tasks, modern AVX-512 vector workloads, or high-bandwidth networking. Instead, it is tailored for enterprise in-memory databases such as SAP HANA, massive Redis or Memcached caching tiers, and large relational database instances requiring extensive buffer pools.

Benchmark profiles indicate modest single-thread execution and average multi-core throughput alongside high cached memory access. The hardware profile is structured specifically for memory-bound deployments, delivering effective resource economics for workloads where RAM capacity dictates system sizing over raw CPU velocity, such as in-memory databases, large-scale caching engines, and enterprise data processing pipelines.
